interactions: Levetiracetam with ipilimumab, nivolumab, dexamethasone, escitalopram or pantoprazole: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; levetiracetam is renally cleared and does not affect CYP enzymes.
Lacosamide with escitalopram: no pharmacokinetic interaction. Lacosamide prolongs the PR interval; escitalopram prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent way; obtain a baseline ECG.
Lacosamide is partly excreted unchanged in urine and partly metabolized (CYP2C19, CYP3A4, CYP2C9); strong CYP2C19 inhibitors can raise its exposure.

Phenytoin, carbamazepine and phenobarbital with dexamethasone: CYP3A4 induction lowers dexamethasone exposure; these inducers also lower the exposure of CYP3A4-metabolized BRAF and MEK inhibitors (for example dabrafenib, encorafenib and cobimetinib) and of escitalopram.
Checkpoint inhibitors (monoclonal antibodies) have no CYP-mediated interactions with antiseizure medications.
output.proposed: Levetiracetam dose increase, or lacosamide as add-on or replacement, with ipilimumab, nivolumab, dexamethasone, escitalopram and pantoprazole
warnings: Levetiracetam: irritability, anxiety and low mood; these can worsen an underlying anxiety disorder and reduce adherence.
Systemic corticosteroids at higher doses may blunt the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitor therapy; use the lowest effective dexamethasone dose.
Escitalopram: hyponatremia (SIADH) is possible, particularly with oxcarbazepine or carbamazepine.

results.summary: Suspected immune-related encephalitis is evaluated with MRI, lumbar puncture (cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, viral PCR, autoimmune and paraneoplastic panels) and EEG to look for subclinical seizures, and alternative causes are excluded; checkpoint inhibitor therapy is held and corticosteroids are given for moderate or severe encephalitis. prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture before imaging has excluded mass effect.
Do not start phenytoin, carbamazepine or phenobarbital: enzyme induction lowers dexamethasone and BRAF/MEK inhibitor exposure.
Do not use zonisamide: it is a sulfonamide and she has a sulfonamide allergy.
Do not start high-dose corticosteroids for presumed checkpoint inhibitor encephalitis: the CSF is non-inflammatory and the seizures are explained by the enlarging metastasis.
Do not attribute the episodes to immunotherapy fatigue or anxiety without treating them as seizures from the metastasis.
required_recommendations: Restore effective non-inducing ASM therapy: address the missed evening doses, and because levetiracetam irritability drives the non-adherence, switch to or add lacosamide (or raise levetiracetam if tolerated).

Discuss with oncology and radiation oncology: stereotactic radiosurgery or resection of the enlarging left temporal metastasis, continuation of ipilimumab and nivolumab, and the lowest effective dexamethasone dose.
Ask radiation oncology to assess the right L3-L4 foraminal metastasis causing the right lumbar radiculopathy (no cord compression).
Repeat TSH and free T4 in 4-6 weeks for checkpoint inhibitor thyroid dysfunction; start levothyroxine if TSH rises above 10, free T4 falls or she becomes symptomatic.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.

avoided_actions.rationale: Episodes with an epigastric aura, deja vu and automatisms witnessed on examination are focal seizures; no murmur, syncope or embolic question for an echocardiogram.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin secondary to left temporal melanoma metastasis (with concurrent suspected immune-related neurotoxicity from checkpoint inhibitors)

differential.key_features: Onset after the second ipilimumab and nivolumab cycle, but the episodes are stereotyped focal seizures from the side of the enlarging metastasis, the CSF has 3 cells with negative antibody panels, and MRI shows no inflammation beyond the perilesional edema.
No leptomeningeal enhancement, negative cytology and flow cytometry, and a normal CSF glucose ratio; a single cytology does not fully exclude it.

Growth during checkpoint inhibitor therapy can be inflammatory, but tripling in size over 4 months with symptomatic edema in a non-irradiated metastasis is managed as progression; follow-up imaging with neuro-oncology settles it.
Weakness and sensory change confined to the right L3-L4 territory with preserved reflexes elsewhere match the right L3-L4 foraminal metastasis, not a polyradiculoneuropathy.
TSH 6.8 with a low-normal free T4 indicates primary thyroid dysfunction rather than hypophysitis; no headache or visual symptoms, and no pituitary abnormality on MRI.
CSF paraneoplastic and neuronal surface antibody panels negative; no bilateral mesial temporal signal.

key_clinical_evidence: Stereotyped episodes with rising epigastric warmth, deja vu and a metallic taste, behavioral arrest, oral and right-hand automatisms and brief postictal confusion, several a day and two witnessed on examination, are focal impaired-awareness seizures of temporal origin.

Contrast MRI shows the known left temporal metastasis grown from 0.5 to 1.6 cm, with edema into the left hippocampal formation, no new lesion and no leptomeningeal enhancement; the routine EEG shows intermittent left temporal slowing.
Levetiracetam 5.9 mcg/mL is below range: she skips evening doses because of irritability.
CSF with 3 cells, mildly raised protein, a normal glucose ratio and negative cytology, flow cytometry and antibody panels argues against checkpoint inhibitor encephalitis and leptomeningeal disease.
The leg weakness follows a right L3-L4 pattern that matches the right L3-L4 foraminal metastasis on the staging spine MRI.
Non-inducing ASMs are preferred because enzyme inducers lower dexamethasone and BRAF/MEK inhibitor exposure.

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Harmon is a 30-year-old right-handed woman with BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic melanoma currently receiving combination immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab who is admitted for evaluation of progressive neurological symptoms. Approximately ten days after her second immunotherapy cycle, she began noticing diffuse fatigue and mild weakness predominantly in her lower extremities, which she and her oncology team initially attributed to treatment-related toxicity. Over the following week, she developed intermittent episodes of unresponsiveness that were first noticed by her partner. During these episodes, she would stop mid-conversation, stare blankly for 15 to 30 seconds, and occasionally make repetitive chewing or lip-smacking movements. She has no recollection of these events and has been dismissing her partner's concerns as exaggeration of ordinary cancer-related fatigue and inattention.

In the past five days, the episodes have become more frequent, now occurring three to five times per day. On two occasions her partner observed her suddenly pause while eating, turn her head slowly to the right, and make fumbling movements with her right hand, followed by approximately one minute of confusion during which she was unable to answer simple questions. She has also described a peculiar sensation that precedes some of the episodes: a rising warmth from her abdomen accompanied by an intense feeling of deja vu and an unusual metallic taste. She initially attributed these sensations to nausea from her immunotherapy but acknowledges that they are distinctly different from the chemotherapy-related nausea she experienced previously.

Her oncology team is primarily concerned about immune-mediated neurotoxicity, specifically an immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated neuropathy or encephalitis, given the temporal relationship between her second immunotherapy cycle and symptom onset. There is also concern about progression of her known left temporal brain metastasis. A staging spine MRI two weeks ago showed vertebral metastases including L2 and L4 with right L3-L4 foraminal tumor, without cord compression or epidural disease; since then she has had intermittent aching in the right groin and anterior thigh. The mild lower extremity weakness adds complexity, as it could represent a concurrent immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy (such as Guillain-Barre syndrome, which has been reported with checkpoint inhibitors), spinal metastatic disease causing early cord compression, or simply deconditioning. She was started on prophylactic levetiracetam when the brain metastasis was first discovered, but adherence has been inconsistent due to side effects of irritability and fatigue. She reports sometimes skipping her evening dose. An outpatient routine EEG performed at the oncology clinic two weeks ago was reportedly normal. She is now admitted to the neurology service for comprehensive evaluation of the paroxysmal episodes and progressive weakness.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a brief episode lasting approximately 20 seconds in which she stopped speaking, appeared to stare blankly to the right, and made repetitive lip-smacking movements. She then resumed conversation but was briefly confused about what had been discussed. She attributed this to fatigue from chemotherapy. A second similar episode of 15 seconds occurred 40 minutes later with an associated hand automatism (picking at the bedsheets with her right hand). She denied awareness of either episode.
